content.title: About
content.content: A bagel is a ring‑shaped yeast‑leavened bread that is boiled briefly before being baked to a golden crust. This version incorporates pieces of fruit (other than raisins), giving it a subtle sweetness and a burst of flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The classic bagel originated in Eastern European Jewish communities in the 19th century.
Bagels are typically boiled in water with a touch of baking soda or honey, which creates their characteristic glossy crust.
Fruit‑filled bagels are popular in the United States and Canada, using apples, cranberries, cherries and other berries.
Bagels are denser than regular bread because of the double cooking process of boiling and baking.
Japan has a similar product called “pankē,” but with a softer texture.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Bagels provide sustained energy thanks to slowly digestible carbohydrates.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole‑wheat dough supplies thiamine, niacin and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Fruit antioxidants
items.content: The added fruit contributes vitamin C, polyphenols and other antioxidants that support immunity.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain flour and fruit pieces increase fiber content, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in trans fats
items.content: Traditional bagel preparation does not involve hydrogenated oils.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Bagels contain wheat, making them unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Because of the dense structure and fruit sugars, bagels can raise blood glucose quickly.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Fruit additions increase total sugar, which should be considered by individuals with diabetes.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Bagels are more calorie‑dense than regular bread, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the bagel in half and spread cream cheese, nut butter or hummus. It pairs well with yogurt, cottage cheese, or as a sandwich with smoked salmon or deli meat. Lightly toasting before serving adds a crunchy crust.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep bagels in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 7 days) or freeze (up to 3 months). Warm in a toaster or oven before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Bulgur is a whole‑grain product made from pre‑cooked, dried and cracked hard wheat. It retains most of the grain’s nutrients, contains no added fat, and has a light nutty flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bulgur is a staple in Middle Eastern dishes such as tabbouleh and kibbeh.
Because it is pre‑cooked, bulgur cooks quickly – just pour hot water over it and let it sit.
It comes in fine, medium and coarse grinds, each suited to different recipes.
Bulgur is high in dietary fiber, which supports digestive health.
Unlike rice, bulgur retains more B‑vitamins.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy bowel function, increases satiety and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Complex carbohydrates provide sustained energy, beneficial for athletes and active individuals.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron is essential for oxygen transport in the blood and for energy metabolism.

items.title: Provides magnesium
items.content: Magnesium supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes bulgur suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Bulgur contains gluten and is not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Like many whole grains, bulgur contains phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption when consumed in excess.

items.title: Food allergies
items.content: Rarely, individuals allergic to wheat may react to bulgur.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bulgur can be added to salads, soups, side dishes, or used as a base for vegetarian patties. To prepare, pour boiling water over the grain (ratio 1:2), cover, and let stand for 10–15 minutes. It can also be toasted dry in a pan to enhance its nutty flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bulgur in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from moisture and light. Properly stored, it remains good for up to a year.

cream-puff-eclair-custard-or-cream-fille.title: Cream puff, eclair, custard or cream filled, iced

content.title: About
content.content: A cream puff (eclair) is a small pastry made from light choux dough, filled with custard or pastry cream and topped with a glaze. The dough is created from water, butter, flour and eggs, while the filling typically consists of vanilla custard, pastry cream, or a flavored cream, sometimes enriched with fruit.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eclairs originated in France in the 17th century; the name comes from the French word “éclair”, meaning “lightning”, because they disappear quickly from the plate.
Traditional filling is pastry cream, but modern recipes often use custard, whipped cream, or mascarpone‑based creams.
Glazes can be chocolate, sugar, or fruit‑based, allowing a wide range of flavor combinations.
Eclairs are a staple in patisseries and cafés, served as individual desserts or as part of a dessert platter.
In Russia, a similar pastry is called “profiterole”, frequently served with chocolate sauce.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Both the choux dough and the cream contain eggs, providing high‑quality protein.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Dairy‑based fillings supply calcium, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Eclairs deliver quick energy from the carbohydrates in the dough and the fats in the cream.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and dairy contribute B2, B12 and other B‑vitamins involved in metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants in chocolate glaze
items.content: When dark chocolate glaze is used, it provides flavonoids with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Egg and dairy allergies
items.content: Eclairs can trigger allergic reactions in individuals sensitive to eggs or lactose.

items.title: High sugar and fat content
items.content: Glaze and cream often contain significant amounts of sugar and saturated fat, which may contribute to weight gain if consumed frequently.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: One cream puff can contain 150–250 kcal, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Trans‑fat presence
items.content: Using margarine instead of butter in the dough may introduce trans fats.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve cream puffs at room temperature; they can be enjoyed as a standalone dessert or alongside coffee or tea. For extra flair, add fresh berries, toasted nuts, or a dusting of powdered sugar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cream puffs in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Allow them to come to room temperature before serving. They can be frozen for up to 2 months if wrapped tightly in plastic film.

content.title: About
content.content: Herring (Clupea harengus) is a marine fish from the Clupeidae family, found in the North Atlantic and Baltic seas. It has a silvery body, a distinctive smell, and firm flesh that is commonly used for pickling, smoking, and in salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Herring is one of the most popular fish in Russia and the Nordic countries.
In the 19th century Sweden introduced a "Herring Day" when pickled herring was traditionally served.
Herring can migrate over 2,000 km in search of feeding grounds.
In the Baltic Sea herring plays a key role in the food chain, serving as a main prey for seabirds and marine mammals.
Herring is a staple in traditional dishes such as "herring under a fur coat" and pickled herring.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Herring provides EPA and DHA, polyunsaturated fatty acids that support heart and brain health.

items.title: High in vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D from herring aids calcium absorption and supports the immune system.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for red blood cell formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Protein‑dense
items.content: Herring supplies a complete set of amino acids useful for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Minerals: selenium and iodine
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant, while iodine supports thyroid function.

items.title: Heavy metal content
items.content: Like many marine fish, herring can accumulate mercury; moderate consumption is advised, especially for pregnant women and children.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Salt in pickled herring
items.content: Pickled herring often contains high amounts of salt, which may be unsuitable for people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Herring can be eaten fresh, smoked, pickled, or canned. It is added to salads, sandwiches, spreads, and traditional dishes such as "herring under a fur coat".

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh herring fillets should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C for up to 2 days. Smoked and pickled herring store in a sealed container in the fridge for up to a week, while canned herring can be kept in a cool, dry place until the expiration date.

content.title: About
content.content: Fried cookie is a small sweet pastry made from dough that is deep‑fried until golden and crisp. It has a crunchy texture, buttery aroma and a mild sweetness. Fried cookies are often used as a base for desserts or enjoyed as a standalone snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fried cookies appeared in Europe in the 19th century as an alternative to baked sweets.
The dough typically contains flour, sugar, eggs, butter, and sometimes spices such as cinnamon, ginger or cardamom.
In some countries these treats are called “fritters” and are served dusted with powdered sugar.
Traditionally they are made in small portions, making them ideal for street vendors.
There are many filling variations – from jam and chocolate to nuts and dried fruit.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates provide quick energy, useful during periods of high activity.

items.title: Contains some protein
items.content: Eggs and dairy in the dough supply a modest amount of animal and plant protein.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: When whole‑grain flour is used, the cookie contains B1, B2 and niacin, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Fried cookies provide iron, magnesium and phosphorus, important for bones and blood formation.

items.title: Antioxidants from spices
items.content: Adding cinnamon or ginger boosts antioxidant content, helping protect cells.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Deep‑frying adds saturated fats, so consumption should be moderate.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: One cookie can contain 80–120 kcal, which matters for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: The dough often contains eggs, milk and gluten, which may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Trans fats from reused oil
items.content: Reusing frying oil can create trans fats, which are harmful to cardiovascular health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve fried cookies warm, dusted with powdered sugar or drizzled with chocolate sauce. They pair well with ice cream, berry coulis, or can be used as a crunchy base for dessert plates.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cookies in an airtight container at room temperature, away from moisture. For longer storage, refrigerate, and for extended periods freeze to preserve their crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Walnuts are the edible seeds of trees of the genus Juglans, most commonly the English or Persian walnut (Juglans regia), native to Central Asia and the Middle East. They are encased in a hard shell inside a green husk and have a wrinkled, brain-like shape. Walnuts have a rich, slightly bitter, earthy flavor and are eaten as a snack and used in baking, salads, sauces, and desserts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Walnuts are among the oldest tree foods known and have been cultivated for thousands of years.
They contain more plant-based omega-3 fatty acids (ALA) than most other nuts.
Black walnuts are a different species with a stronger flavor and a very hard shell.
The walnut's wrinkled shape has long been compared to the human brain.
Walnut oil is used in cooking, especially as a finishing oil.

items.title: Rich in ALA omega-3
items.content: Walnuts are one of the best plant sources of alpha-linolenic acid, an omega-3 fatty acid.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Walnuts contain polyphenols, especially in their papery skin, with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Provides fiber and protein
items.content: Walnuts contribute fiber and plant protein, which support fullness.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Walnuts contain magnesium, copper, and manganese.

items.title: Heart-friendly fats
items.content: Walnuts contain mostly polyunsaturated fats, which can be part of a heart-friendly diet.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Walnuts can cause allergic reactions, which may be severe in some people.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Walnuts are calorie-dense, so portions should be moderate.

items.title: Rancidity and mold
items.content: Old walnuts can turn rancid, and moldy nuts can contain harmful toxins and should be discarded.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Whole walnuts are not suitable for young children because they can cause choking.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Walnuts can be eaten as a snack, chopped into salads, oatmeal, yogurt, and baked goods such as banana bread and brownies, or ground into sauces and pesto. Toasting them lightly brings out their flavor and reduces bitterness. Choose unsalted walnuts when possible.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store shelled walnuts in an airtight container in the refrigerator or freezer, where their oils stay fresh for longer. Walnuts in the shell keep for several months in a cool, dry place. Discard walnuts that smell rancid or taste bitter, or that look moldy.

content.title: About
content.content: Yeast extract spread is a concentrated product made from autolyzed cells of the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. It has a strong umami flavor, with a slightly salty and mildly sweet note, and is often used as a flavor enhancer, cheese substitute, or sauce base.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Commercial production of yeast extract began in the early 20th century in Japan under the brand “Miso”.
It is rich in B‑vitamins, especially B12, which is rare in plant‑based foods.
The spread is popular in vegetarian and vegan cuisine as a cheese‑like flavor enhancer.
High glutamic acid content provides natural umami without added MSG.
In some countries it is classified as a food additive, in others as a ready‑to‑eat product.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Yeast extract contains thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, vitamin B6 and folate, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: About 10 g of plant protein are present per 100 g of spread, making it a useful addition to vegetarian diets.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Beta‑glucans in yeast can stimulate immune cells and improve resistance to infections.

items.title: Enhances flavor with less salt
items.content: The umami taste allows reduction of added salt in dishes, beneficial for blood‑pressure management.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Autolysis partially breaks down yeast cells, making the nutrients more readily absorbable.

items.title: Yeast allergy
items.content: People allergic to yeast or fermented products may experience skin rash, swelling, or gastrointestinal symptoms.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Some spreads contain up to 1 g of sodium per 100 g, so individuals monitoring salt intake should limit portions.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Yeast extract is high in purines, which can be problematic for gout or hyperuricemia sufferers.

items.title: Glutamate sensitivity
items.content: Although glutamate is natural, sensitive individuals may experience headaches or a tingling sensation after large amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spread can be used on bread, mixed into sauces, soups, marinades, vegan “cheese” dishes, or added to smoothies for a flavor boost. Keep refrigerated and stir before use, as oil may separate.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the spread in a sealed container in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C. Shelf life is typically 12 months after opening. Discard if the smell, color, or texture changes or if mold appears.

content.title: About
content.content: Yellow string beans are edible pods of the common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) that have a bright yellow color and are prepared by boiling. They have a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a tender texture, making them popular in side dishes, salads, and soups.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Yellow beans differ from green beans only in pod color, but share a similar nutritional profile.
They are traditionally cultivated in warm regions of North and South America as well as Europe.
Ancient varieties were used by Indigenous peoples long before European colonization.
When cooked, the beans retain most of their B‑vitamins and minerals.
Yellow beans can serve as a lower‑calorie alternative to starchy side dishes.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps maintain healthy blood sugar levels.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Yellow beans contain virtually no fat, making them suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving of cooked beans provides about 7 g of protein, beneficial for vegetarians and vegans.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B6, and folate aid energy metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Minerals: iron and magnesium
items.content: Iron contributes to hemoglobin formation, while magnesium supports muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans, ranging from skin rashes to severe symptoms.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking beans before cooking helps mitigate this.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Beans can cause bloating in sensitive people; gradual introduction to the diet lessens the effect.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked yellow string beans can be tossed into salads, soups, stews, used as a side dish for meat or fish, or incorporated into vegetable casseroles. They can also be quickly sautéed with garlic and herbs for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked beans in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze them in portioned bags for up to 3 months. Discard any beans that develop an off‑smell or mold.
